en: Imperial Edict: I, the Emperor, reflect that as for the three teachings’ awakening of the people within the realm, their principles issue from a single source and their paths proceed side by side without contradiction.
It is only because people are unable to achieve a sudden, penetrating realization that they each harbor different intentions and maintain different views.
Those who admire the Dao claim that Buddhism is not as venerable as Daoism; those who turn toward Buddhism claim that Daoism is not as... [as venerable as Buddhism].
The Buddha is great; yet Confucianists further exclude the two [Buddhist and Daoist] traditions, regarding them as heterodox.
Clutching their private biases, they contend and vie for victory, refusing to yield to one another. I, for my part, maintain the discourse on the Three Teachings solely to achieve balance.
When balance is attained, one overlooks external differences in form and appearance while internally verifying the commonality of fundamental nature and principle. And...
One knows that the three teachings have never differed in their fundamental intent; they are all nothing other than desiring that people return together to goodness.

Now, the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Actions of the Buddha guide people toward goodness. As for the Five Constant Virtues and the hundredfold conduct of our Confucianism, which encourage, assist, and exhort us—how could there be even one among them that does not lead people to do good?
Formerly, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty asked the Palace Attendant He Shangzhi: "The Six..."
The scriptures are fundamentally for the salvation of the world. As for the essential truths of the spirit, one takes the Buddhist sutras as the guiding compass.
If the people throughout the land were all to be purified by this transformation, then I would achieve Great Peace while sitting still. Heshang Zhi replied:

"In a village of a hundred households, if ten people uphold the five precepts, those ten will become pure and prudent. In a town of a thousand houses, if a hundred people uphold the ten [precepts]..."

If there is goodness, then the hundred clans will be harmonious. If this moral instruction is maintained and spread throughout the world, then among the billions of registered households, there will be millions of benevolent people.
If one can perform a single good deed, one evil is removed; if one evil is removed, one instance of punishment ceases.
When one punishment ceases within the family, ten thousand punishments cease within the state. Truly, it is possible to achieve great peace while sitting with arms folded.
These words are intended to encourage goodness, for it is the essential way to govern the world.
The Buddhist transformation of greed and stinginess, and its inducement of the virtuous, likewise has its purpose rooted in this.

If one were to believe and follow them, they could truly serve as a model for the upright and a lesson for the common people, becoming a great aid in serving the sovereign and benefiting the populace. To arbitrarily disparage them and recklessly fabricate [accusations] against them...

Those who debate the doctrines of Yang Zhu and Mo Di have all failed to perceive the true color [of the truth]; their arguments are merely the blind ravings of those who have lost their way. Special Instruction.

The Essential Points of the Sutra on the Ten Wholesome Courses of Action (with an appended explanation of the retributions for the ten unwholesome courses of action). The fifteenth day of the second month, the eleventh year of the Yongzheng reign.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ouyi: On Abstaining from Taking Life.
One attains ten methods for being free from affliction: first, universally bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
second, constantly giving rise to a mind of great compassion toward sentient beings; third, forever severing all habitual tendencies of anger and resentment; fourth, the body...
1. One is always free from illness. 2. Fifth, one’s lifespan is long and far-reaching. 3. Sixth, one is constantly protected by non-human beings. 4.

Seventh, one never has bad dreams and experiences joy upon waking from sleep. 5. Eighth, one eliminates the knots of enmity, and all hostilities are naturally resolved. 6. Ninth, one has no fear of the evil realms. 7.
Tenth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens.
By committing the act of killing, one incurs ten kinds of afflictive conditions: first, one universally instills fear in all sentient beings;
second, one constantly gives rise to a mind of great malice toward sentient beings; third, it is difficult to sever the habitual tendencies of all anger;
fourth, the body is constantly plagued by illness; fifth, one’s lifespan is short; sixth, one is perpetually tormented and harmed by non-human spirits; seventh, one is constantly...
1. Bad dreams; 2. lack of joy upon waking from sleep; 3. the eight difficulties; 4. the removal of resentment and the resolution of various fears; 5.
fear of the evil destinies within the nine states of existence; 6. rebirth in the evil realms at the end of life.

By abstaining from theft, one achieves ten qualities that inspire confidence: first, one’s wealth and resources are abundant and cannot be dissipated by kings, thieves, fire, water, or unworthy heirs;
second, many people hold one in affection; third, others do not deceive or oppress one;
fourth, one is praised in all directions; fifth, one has no anxiety regarding harm; sixth, one’s good reputation spreads abroad; and seventh, one is fearless when among the assembly.

[By abstaining from stealing, one attains] eight things: wealth, life-span, physical beauty, strength, happiness, eloquence, and being fully endowed without deficiency; ninth, always harboring a mind intent on giving;
tenth, being reborn in heaven after death.
By committing theft, one incurs ten kinds of conditions that cannot be relied upon: first, although one’s resources may be overflowing and accumulated, kings and thieves [will seize them].
1. Water and fire, as well as unwelcome children, can all cause dispersal and destruction. 2. Many people harbor thoughts of dislike. 3. Three types of people are able to deceive and oppress one.
4. One is slandered from the four quarters. 5. One constantly suffers the harm of anxiety. 6. An evil reputation spreads abroad. 7. One has fear when among a multitude. 8.
Wealth, life, complexion, and strength are unstable; one lacks eloquence and is deficient. 9. One does not...
With a mind intent on giving, one avoids ten rebirths in the evil destinies at the end of life.
By abstaining from sexual misconduct, one attains four qualities praised by the wise: first, the faculties are well-tamed and compliant; second, one is forever free from clamor and agitation;
third, one is lauded by the world; and fourth, one’s wife cannot be violated by others.
Committing sexual misconduct results in four kinds of states not praised by the wise: first, the sense faculties are not disciplined; second, one is not free from agitation and restlessness;
third, one is loathed by the world; and fourth, one's wife is constantly susceptible to being violated.
By abstaining from false speech, one attains eight qualities praised by humans and devas: first, one’s mouth is perpetually pure, and the tongue-root has the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus;
second, one is trusted and believed by all the world; third, one’s words are taken as truthful testimony, and one is revered by humans and devas;
fourth, one constantly comforts sentient beings with loving speech; fifth, one attains a superior intention, and the three karmic actions are purified.
Sixth, his speech is free from error, and his mind is always joyful. Seventh, his words are respected, and both humans and devas follow them.
Eighth, his wisdom is preeminent and cannot be overcome by any.

By committing false speech, one incurs eight qualities that are not praised by humans or devas: first, the mouth is perpetually impure, and the root of the tongue is foul-smelling and pervasive with stench;
second, one is not trusted by the world; third, one’s words lack sincerity and proof, and thus one is not respected by humans or devas;
fourth, one constantly harms sentient beings with malicious speech; fifth, one acquires inferior mental karma—[thus completing] the three types of karma.
1. Impurity. 2. Constantly erring in speech. 3. The mind is perpetually sorrowful. 4. Speech is frivolous;
humans and devas do not follow it. 5. Wisdom is inferior; people are able to subdue it.
By refraining from double-tongued speech, one attains five kinds of qualities that cannot be lost: first, one attains an indestructible body, because no one can harm it;
second, one attains an indestructible retinue, because no one can cause division; third, one attains unshakable faith, because one accords with one’s original karma;
fourth, one attains indestructible practice of the Dharma, because what is cultivated is firm and solid; fifth, one attains indestructible spiritual friends, because they do not deceive.

Due to delusion, one commits the offense of double-tongued speech (slander) and acquires five kinds of destructible qualities: first, one acquires that which can destroy the body, because there is the capacity to cause harm;

second, one acquires that which can destroy one's retinue, because there is the capacity to cause division; third, one acquires that which can destroy faith, because it violates one’s fundamental vocation; fourth, one acquires...
One is able to destroy the practice of the Dharma because that which is cultivated lacks firmness. Fifth, one encounters corrupt spiritual friends who constantly deceive and mislead.

Regarding the precept against harsh speech, one achieves the accomplishment of eight kinds of pure karma: first, one’s words do not deviate from the [bodhisattva] vows; second, all one’s words are beneficial.
First, his words always accord with the truth. Second, his phrasing is exquisite. Third, his words are readily understood. Fourth, his words are trusted and relied upon.
Fifth, his words are beyond reproach. Sixth, his words are entirely pleasing.
One commits the offense of harsh speech and fails to accomplish the eight kinds of pure karma: first, one's speech constantly deviates from the proper measure;

second, one's speech is not beneficial; third, one's speech does not accord with principle; fourth, one's words are coarse and rugged; fifth, one's words are difficult to comprehend; sixth, one's words are not trusted or believed;
seventh, one's words are frequently subject to ridicule; eighth, one's words are entirely unpleasant.
By refraining from frivolous speech, one achieves three kinds of certainty: first, one will certainly be beloved by the wise;

second, one will certainly be able to answer questions according to reality through wisdom; and third, one will certainly possess supreme majesty and virtue among humans and devas, being free from falsehood.
One commits frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). One fails to achieve three kinds of certainty: first, one is certainly censured by those possessed of wisdom;
second, one is certainly unable to answer questions with wisdom as they truly are; third, one is certainly inferior in power and majesty to humans and devas, and is definitely subject to falsehood.
Appendix: One Article on the Precept Against Alcohol from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

By abstaining from alcohol, one achieves ten kinds of faultless qualities: first, one’s complexion does not become unsightly; second, one does not lose physical strength; third, one’s vision remains clear;
fourth, one manifests no signs of anger or resentment; fifth, one’s fields, enterprises, and means of livelihood are not ruined.

1. Dharma. 2. One does not contract diseases. 3. One does not increase quarrels or litigation. 4. One does not have a reputation for evil; rather, a good reputation spreads. 5. Wisdom does not diminish. 6. One does not fall ill. 7. One does not increase disputes or lawsuits. 8. There is no spread of ill repute;
instead, a good name circulates. 9. Wisdom does not decrease. 10. At the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one does not fall into the three evil realms.
By consuming alcohol, one incurs ten kinds of faulty conditions: first, an ugly complexion; second, diminished strength; third, unclear vision;
fourth, manifesting signs of anger; fifth, the ruin of fields, livelihoods, and means of subsistence;
sixth, the increase of diseases; seventh, the promotion of strife and litigation; eighth, the spread of ill repute instead of good fame; ninth, [the loss of] wisdom...
[These] decrease. When the body breaks up at the end of life, one falls into the three evil realms.
By restraining greed for sensual desires, one attains the accomplishment of five kinds of mastery: first, mastery over the three types of action, whereby the sense faculties are fully endowed;
second, mastery over material wealth, whereby no enemies or thieves can seize it; third, mastery over merit, whereby all desired objects are provided according to one's wishes.

Fourth, one attains sovereignty over the rank of the Four Heavenly Kings, and all rare and wondrous things are offered to them. Fifth, the excellent objects obtained exceed what was originally sought.
[By] committing the transgression of covetousness, one fails to achieve five kinds of mastery: first, the impurity of the three karmas and the deficiency of the sense faculties;
second, lack of mastery over wealth and property, such that all enemies and thieves can seize it; third, lack of mastery over merit and virtue, as they do not follow one's desires.
It is difficult to provide for all necessities. One lacks sovereignty over the rank of a Caturmahārājika king. One must offer up rare and precious things that are difficult to obtain.
Fifth, the objects obtained are inferior and not what was originally sought.
By refraining from ill-will (*vyāpāda*), one attains eight kinds of mental states of joy: first, a mind free from harm; second, a mind free from ill-will.
Third, a mind free from contention and dispute; fourth, a mind that is gentle, supple, and upright; fifth, the attainment of a noble mind of loving-kindness;
sixth, a mind that constantly acts for the benefit and peace of sentient beings; seventh, having physical features that are dignified and majestic, such that all hold them in reverence;
eighth, by virtue of harmony and patience, swiftly being reborn in the Brahma-world.
By committing acts of anger, one cannot attain the eight factors of a joyful mind: first, a mind of harmful affliction; second, a mind of resentment; third, a mind of contention;
fourth, a mind that is coarse, arrogant, and devious; fifth, a mind of ordinary malice;

sixth, a failure to cultivate a mind that benefits and brings peace to sentient beings; seventh, a physical appearance that is not dignified, such that the multitude does not respect one; eighth, by...
Because they are coarse and violent, they quickly fall into the evil realms.
Through precepts, right views, and freedom from delusion, one attains ten meritorious qualities: first, one attains a truly virtuous intention and true spiritual companions;
second, one has deep faith in cause and effect, such that one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever commit an evil deed; third, one takes refuge in the Buddha alone.
1. Not being among other devas and so forth; 2. Possessing a straightforward mind and right view, forever free from the net of doubts regarding all matters of fortune and misfortune;
3. Constantly being reborn among humans and devas, never again falling into the evil realms; 4. Having immeasurable merit and wisdom that increase more and more in excellence;

5. Forever leaving behind false paths and practicing the noble path; 6. Not giving rise to the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and abandoning all evil karma; 7. Abiding in non-obstruction.
They see ten things: first, they do not fall into the various states of suffering;

second, they do not commit the view of perverse delusion; third, they do not fail to accomplish the ten dharmas of merit; fourth, they do not lose their genuine and wholesome aspiration or their genuine and wholesome companions;

fifth, they do not lack faith in cause and effect; sixth, they would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than ultimately commit evil; seventh, they do not take refuge solely in non-Buddhist paths; [and so forth].
1. Other devas and so forth; 2. A crooked mind and wrong views, making it difficult to escape the net of doubt regarding all matters of fortune and misfortune;
3. Constantly reborn in the evil realms, never again reaching the good paths; 4. Immeasurable false wisdom that increases and intensifies further and further;

5. Permanently departing from the right path and practicing non-paths; 6. Constantly giving rise to the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) and abandoning all wholesome karma; 7. Abiding in obstructed views.
Ten Constant Falls into Adversity.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ouyi (Lianchi) from the Ten Realms of Good and Evil and the Chapter on Karmic Paths.
If, during the ten grave evil deeds of the superior grade,

one clings to the notions of self and person from moment to moment, acting solely for fame and profit, benefiting oneself while harming others, and failing to reflect upon the consequences; if one’s actions of body, speech,
and mind follow purely the habits of delusion, lacking faith in the Triple Gem and violating the precepts of ritual conduct— such are the causes of error.
As for the result: to kill or harm that which is revered is called a karmic path of hell.

If one commits the ten evil deeds of medium grade, and in every moment of thought clings to the notions of self and person, indulges exclusively in sensual desires, and lacks shame or remorse, being as blind as one who has no sight—
Dawn! [Those who are] mired in the darkness of ignorance and folly, possessing many enmities and fetters—this is called the animal realm path of karma.

If one commits the ten evil deeds of the lower grade, even for a single moment of thought, recklessly clinging to the notions of self and person, being stingy, greedy, jealous, and envious, and failing to know how to plant roots of merit, but only accumulating transgressions.
Roots. These are called the karmic paths of the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Even if one practices the ten wholesome actions of the lower grade, if at every moment of thought one harbors a mind of flattery and deception, lacks an upright intention, and outwardly displays benevolence and righteousness while inwardly calculating for the sake of the self—[this constitutes the path of the hungry ghosts].
If a person performs various deeds with a mind intent on victory or defeat, this is called the karmic path of the asuras.
If, during the ten intermediate wholesome acts,
one’s every thought is marked by the fear of falling into suffering, and one restrains the five desires, upholds the mind in the precepts, and aspires for the future—
There is. This is called the path of action of the human realm.

If, within every moment of thought, one possesses the superior grade of the ten wholesome courses of action with outflows, and vows: "In the future, may I always experience supreme bliss and extensively perform various merits," thereby restraining all [unwholesome states]...
From the cessation of transgressions up to the gathering of the distracted mind into dhyāna, and the disparaging of form to enter emptiness—this is called the path of action of the celestial realm.

If, within every moment of thought, one contemplates the suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self of the three realms with supreme, untainted ten wholesome deeds, relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness... [deeply...]
Believing in dependent origination, they forever sever the desire for future existence and resolve solely upon the bliss of cessation and the unconditioned;
this is called the path of karma of the two vehicles (which includes the śrāvakas).
Furthermore, within each moment of thought, those who possess the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths— whether tainted or untainted—

give rise to great compassion by taking the two truths of suffering and its origin as their object, and give rise to great loving-kindness by taking the two truths of the path and cessation as their object.
They deeply contemplate the emptiness of both self and phenomena, and out of pity for sentient beings who are mired in delusion, they employ various skillful means to...
That awakening pervades the worlds of the ten directions without limitation; it continues until the end of the future without weariness;
it seeks no reward of gratitude, plots no fame, hopes for no recognition by others, and perceives neither subject nor object. This is called the bodhisattva’s path of action.

Neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, when one contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena within each moment of thought—even while practicing the ten supreme wholesome deeds—the provisional is identical to the real, and principle and phenomenon are equal;

the real is identical to the provisional, and the thousand suchnesses are distinct. In stillness there is constant function, and as the myriad practices arise like clouds, in function there is constant stillness. One.
The limit is itself limitless. One does not form the notion of "one," nor does one form the notion of "all. Yet, one is able to realize that the one is all and all is one;
that lands as numerous as motes of dust are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip; and that the ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment of thought.

The body pervades the ten directions yet undergoes neither union nor dispersion; wisdom enters the three periods of time yet involves neither coming nor going. This is called the path of karma of the Buddha-realm.
